items.content:
Standing up a new centralized Procurement department is crazy hard....

In addition to finding the optimal combination of People, Process and Technology,

you have to educate everyone else in the organization about why good Procurement is valuable...

Why centralization makes sense...

This can take YEARS from when you start... (3 movies in fact... 😅)

Even when you have a strong Board/CEO mandate...

If you've been working in Procurement a long time, this can be incredibly frustrating...

"Nobody realizes the value we am bringing to the organization! They see us as red tape!"

That being said, it's one of the most rewarding things you can do in your Procurement career.

So what's the solution?

➝ Be very clear and concise with your function's objectives and how they relate to the overall company values and mission.

➝ Build a great team who "gets it."

➝ Start small, focusing on getting a few "big wins" to get momentum going.

➝ Build out clear processes supported by the best tech you can manage to stay nimble.

➝ Keep repeating yourself... over and over again, staying humble. It makes a difference.

➝ Listen to your users (e.g. via an internal Procurement community) and iterate based on feedback 

➝ Set bigger objectives as you grow your influence and accumulate wins.

Great procurement functions are built one step at a time.

And then, before you realize it, you're standing in front of mount doom,

throwing in the "decentralized, immature purchasing" ring.... 😅

items.content:
The reason your last implementation ran late has a name. And it's not the consulting partner's name 😅

Bent Flyvbjerg studied 16,000+ different types of projects across 136 countries.

Only 8.5% finished on time and on budget.

Add "delivered the promised benefits" to that bar, and it drops to 0.5%.

IT projects fall squarely in this distribution...

The culprit isn't incompetence.

It's a cognitive pattern Flyvbjerg and Daniel Kahneman call the planning fallacy.

Most timelines get built from the "inside out".

List the tasks. Assign durations. Add a 15% buffer.

This ignores how similar projects actually performed in the past.

The fix is Reference Class Forecasting.

Start from the historical record, not your project plan.

→ Find deployments comparable to yours in scope
→ Pull actual outcome data, not vendor reference calls
→ Position your project in that range, adjust at the margins

Do that, and you'll have much better data about how long your project will take.

There's also a second problem: your RFP process rewards the vendor who lowballs the timeline.

(which inevitably gets you into trouble)

Everyone knows it. Everyone plays along anyway.

I break down where to find your reference class data and what to ask your consulting partner in the latest ProcureTech Unpacked episode.

items.content:
I don't want to hear about another "AI-powered" solution... I'm done. 

Artificial Intelligence just means "computer systems that can perform tasks mimicking human-like intelligence" 

Stuff like recognizing patterns, making predictions, understanding language, and learning from experience.

So when vendors tell you their solution is "AI-powered," they're essentially saying "our solution runs on computers." 

How... helpful? 😂

Unless vendors start talking to you about the types of AI being used, they're telling you nothing useful.

Machine Learning for spend classification?
Natural Language Processing for contract review?
Computer Vision for invoice processing?

NOW we're talking.

Here's my vendor grilling framework:

Don't care about tech details? Focus on outcomes.

→ Does it cut contract review time by 50%?

→ Does it catch duplicate payments?

→ What's the measurable impact?

→ Give me the references!!

Want to dig deeper? Learn and ask about specific AI types and how they are stitched together.

→ "We use AI" = meaningless

→ "We use NLP for clause extraction with 87% accuracy" = better

Then you can lookup the strengths/weaknesses for that type and get to "real talk"

Real "AI solutions" tell you exactly what they do, in which sequence and understand how it solves your exact problem.

...And then they prove it with numbers, data and references.

Everything else is just expensive buzzword soup.

(and it doesn't even taste good!)

items.content:
OCR isn't Accounts Payable Automation. It's one-sixth of it.
  
Ask ten people what "AP automation" means and you'll get ten different answers.
  
Most stop at "scanning invoices instead of typing them in."
  
That's OCR. It's a feature, not the system.
  
It's also why so many AP automation projects deliver less than half of what the sales call promised.
  
Real AP automation is six steps, not one:
  
→ Invoice receipt
→ Data capture
→ Coding
→ Matching (2-way or 3-way)
→ Approval routing
→ Payment and reconciliation
  
The automation isn't any single step.

It's the invoice moving from step one to step six without anyone re-typing anything along the way.
  
Here's the part vendor demos never show you:
  
PO-based invoices are the easy 80%.

A PO already exists, so the system matches and flags discrepancies automatically.
  
Non-PO invoices (utilities, subscriptions, one-off charges) have nothing to match against.

They rely entirely on your coding rules and approval hierarchy.
  
That's where exception queues balloon and touchless rates stall out.
  
If a demo only shows you clean PO matches, ask to see the non-PO workflow.

That's the part that's actually hard.

There are now 105+ LLM providers in the world.

You've heard of ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, XAI and Gemini.

But the interesting ones are the ones you haven't.

Here are 10 flying under the radar:

→ Mistral AI (France) — Mistral, Mixtral 
→ Cohere (Canada) — Command R+
→ Meta (USA) — Llama (open source)
→ DeepSeek (China) — DeepSeek R1
→ Databricks (USA) — DBRX
→ Aleph Alpha (Germany) — Luminous, Pharia
→ AI21 Labs (USA) — Jamba
→ Alibaba (China) — Qwen
→ Together AI (USA) — inference platform for open models
→ LightOn (France) — Alfred

The golden age of cheap AI access is slowly coming to an end.

Frontier model token costs are rising.

Enterprise AI budgets are getting scrutinized.

Organizations that binged on GPT-4 during the free-money era are now asking harder questions.

Here's what that means for procurement pros:

→ Cost: a fine-tuned small model can do a narrow task better and cheaper than a frontier model

→ Sovereignty: EU and Canadian orgs can't always send data to a US hyperscaler

→ Risk: your ProcureTech vendor betting on one LLM is a single point of failure

→ Leverage: if you can BYOLLM, you can negotiate on AI costs — not just software fees

The next wave of sophisticated buyers won't just ask "does it have AI?"

They'll ask: "which LLM is under the hood, and can we swap it out at will?"

Have you started asking your vendors that question yet?

items.content:
Your S2P platform will never replace your ERP if you do direct purchasing...
 
And yet, I keep seeing companies try.
 
Here's why it never works:
 
Direct purchasing is tied directly to your operations:
 
→ Bills of Materials (BOMs)
→ MRP production schedules
→ Inventory replenishment
→ Engineering change orders
→ Supplier quality management
 
Every one of these lives inside your ERP (or should).
 
Your S2P platform doesn't know what your production line needs next Tuesday.
 
Your ERP does.
 
This is why the "one platform for all procurement" pitch collapses the moment direct spend enters the room.
 
Direct and indirect have different masters:
 
→ Indirect answers to Finance
→ Direct answers to Operations
 
S2P tools were mostly built for indirect.

Great for services, catalog widgets and tail spend.
 
Ask them to handle BOM-driven purchasing with MRP integration and watch the demo go quiet.
 
Making a ProcureTech roadmap in a direct procurement business is a COMPLETELY different game than businesses without:

→ MRP
→ Materials
→ Inventory
 
Companies that fight this fact spend years in failed S2P suite implementations.
 
Companies that accept it do the hard ERP optimization work and build stacks AROUND ERP that actually work.
 
Does your org try to run direct P2P spend through your S2P tool?

How's that going?

items.content:
Direct procurement always gets a worse deal than indirect procurement. That's just the way it is.

When it comes to procurement technology,

I see these 2 mistakes constantly:
 
1) Direct manufacturers buy and end-to-end S2P suites built for indirect-only teams.

Why?

It seems easier than trying to fix the ERP processes... A shortcut!

But it's a mistake in most cases...
 
2) Indirect-only companies running procurement in an ERP with a poor user experience...

When there are such better options out there to get desired benefits.

Seems like a way to save money on applications... But it creates cost elsewhere.
 
Both of these mistakes are expensive ways to create more problems than you solve.
 
Here are the default rules for foundational procurement platforms (even though yes, there are exceptions):
 
→ No inventory, materials or MRP (indirect only)? Put end-to-end procurement in a dedicated platform.
 
→ Inventory, materials and MRP (some direct)? Put P2P inside your ERP. Augment around the edges. Yes, even for indirect spend.
 
Why the second rule surprises people:
 
Your ERP already owns production planning, maintenance, supplier confirmations, and the data manufacturing depends on.
 
Fragmenting purchases across system types doesn't reduce risk. It multiplies it.
 
Even a "bad" ERP beats a disconnected best-of-breed stack if your business runs on inventory and materials.
 
The fix is making the ERP (and the experience around it) better.

A few examples:
 
→ Catalog management integrated with requisitioning
→ Supplier PO confirmation workflows that sit on top of ERP
→ A UX layer that doesn't fight the system underneath it
(or copy database tables...)

items.content:
This is the most hilarious thing I've seen in a while... And it's a perfect analogy for AI Agents.

A Chinese robot recently tried to moonwalk at a tech showcase.

Impressively nailed the first few steps.

Then hit a stair.

Went face-first onto the stage.

The owner had to drag it off by hand.

The crowd's silence was deafening 😅

(The music just keeps going and going...)

Here's the takeaway:

→ AI-supported tech is genuinely remarkable.  What it did before the stairs? Jaw-dropping. Don't let the fall fool you.

→ On a clear path, it performs brilliantly.  No obstacles = no problems. The results can look magical.

→ But it's GUESSING.  Most fields of AI are statistics-based. They predicts the most likely next move based on objective and pattern dataset ("skills"). It's not great with novel problems (e.g. stairs)

→ Your job isn't to be amazed. It's to catch the robot before he falls. It's to remove the stairs ahead of time. And/Or to include the stairs in the dataset for next time.

Guardrails. Human review checkpoints. Edge-case testing. Exception handling. Escalation logic.

That's the real work in the Era of AI...

Getting intimate with the work, as I call it.

The robot didn't fail because it's bad technology.

It failed because nobody mapped the stage.

AI *simulates* human intelligence.

There will be skill level variations (and stupidity) just like with all of us 😅!

It's important never to forget that.

Before you deploy an AI Agent in your procurement process, make sure you're also using showcases (testing!)

And I hope your testing phases provide as many laughs as this video 😂

items.content:
Most procurement pros haven't heard of MCP servers yet. That's a massive missed opportunity.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the new standard that lets AI tools connect directly to your live business systems.

You can literally connect an LLM to your backend systems in 10 minutes (I've done it myself).

No more copy-pasting data into Claude.
No more static exports.
No more AI working blind.
No expensive point-to-point interfaces.

Your AI assistant can now talk directly to your ERP, your S2P suite, your CLM, etc.

(e.g. your contract repository, your supplier database, your transactions - in real time.)

It can also talk with your subscriptions like D&B, Moody's, etc.

Here's what that unlocks for procurement teams right now:

→ Ask your AI to pull live supplier risk scores, contract expiry dates, and spend data — without touching a single report

→ Draft an RFP using your actual historical awards, preferred clauses, and category specs — pulled straight from your systems

→ Route intake requests correctly the first time by connecting your intake tool to your approved supplier list and GL codes automatically

What do you need to make it work?

A ProcureTech software vendor that has a good list of APIs

(e.g. Pull POs, Pull  Contracts, Pull Suppliers, etc.)

And has combined them all in an MCP Server and made it available to you.

You don't need to rebuild your tech stack to benefit.

MCP works as a layer on top of what you already have.

This is the shift from "AI that answers questions" to "AI that does the work."

Procurement teams who figure this out in 2026 will look like superheroes to their stakeholders.

Those who don't will still be exporting spreadsheets.

Which side do you want to be on?

items.content:
Negotiating yearly procurement contracts is a mistake:
 
You work hard. You lock in the best deal.

For a whole year!
 
Then the world moves on without you.
 
A lot can change in 12 months:
 
→ Global events rewrite prices overnight.
→ Suppliers merge, your leverage drops.
→ Your volumes shift. Your plan changes.
→ A better supplier shows up. You can't touch them.
 
You're stuck.
Paying last year's price.
For today's problem.
 
Here's what most teams miss:
 
Yearly contracts make sense when supply is your top risk.
 
Rare metals. Custom parts. Long-lead items.
 
Can't risk a supply gap? Lock it in.
 
But for most spend?
 
Stop putting energy into yearly deals.
 
Start building the skill to check the market on demand:
 
→ Live RFQs and auctions
→ Marketplace spot buys for indirect and tail spend
→ Cost models tied to real-time commodity data
→ Fast sourcing events, done in 48 hours

While capturing and maintaining high quality data.
 
That's the real edge.
 
Not: "I got 5% off a deal I can't leave."
 
But: "I can go to market in 48 hours (or instantly with a marketplace) and get today's best price."
 
Speed beats lock-in. Every time.
 
Is your team set up to check the market on demand?

Or are you still stuck endlessly renewing last year's deal?

items.content:
Your procurement negotiations are failing before they even begin...

Not because you lack skill.

But because you skipped preparation.

It's powerful and romantic to think your negotiation skills can deliver "on-demand"...

...That you're Gordon Gekko but better looking... 😅

Everyone loves talking about "win-win" outcomes.

But here's what preparation actually looks like for most buyers:

→ A rough pricing model thrown together last minute
→ Last year's contract dug out of a shared drive
→ A "can do" attitude that you'll figure it out in the meeting

Spoiler: You're leaving value on the table...

Great negotiation isn't about who outmaneuvers the other in the moment...

It's about who shows up knowing:

→ Their walkaway point
→ Their non-negotiables
→ Their leverage points
→ What your supplier values and what you can give away

And whether your stakeholders are actually aligned on all of it.

This is why I love what Tanya W. put together.

7 negotiation frameworks every procurement pro should know cold.

BATNA. ZOPA. Anchoring. Negotiation styles.

These aren't academic concepts.

They're the difference between stumbling through an IKEA build without the instructions vs. building the Billy bookshelf in 12 minutes flat.

One leaves you with extra screws and a wobbly shelf, swearing.

The other gets you the deal you actually wanted 😅

items.content:
Every manufacturer I talk to right now is having the reshoring conversation. Most of them are having the wrong one.
The wrong conversation: "Should we move production out of China?" The right conversation: "What's our actual exposure, and how do we reduce it without blowing up the supply chain?"
I've moved 121 SKUs from China. Here's what I've seen go wrong when companies skip the second question:
Panic reshoring is the most expensive version. New tariff gets announced. CEO calls an emergency meeting. Someone gets the mandate to "find domestic suppliers — fast." Three months later, they've moved 10 SKUs at a 30% cost premium, quality isn't dialed in, and they've burned through the engineering team's bandwidth on firefighting instead of qualification. I've seen this happen more than once in the last year.
Here's what the right version looks like:
You start with the math. Map every SKU by tariff exposure, sourcing difficulty, and production criticality. Rank them. That ranked list becomes your project plan.
You build inventory before you move anything. We built 18 months of safety stock before we transferred a single mold. Expensive? Yeah. But it's the decision that lets you move at the right pace instead of urgent pace.
You move the knowledge, not just the contract. Molds, setup notes, first article inspection history — all of it. Most reshoring fails because companies switch suppliers and leave the institutional knowledge with the old vendor.
You do the full cost math. Domestic unit cost is almost always higher. But tariffs, freight, lead time, quality escapes, problem resolution — when you add it all up, the net was 12% cheaper for us.
The manufacturers who are going to come out ahead aren't the ones who move fastest. They're the ones who move most deliberately.
Are you reshoring strategically or reactively?
#Reshoring #SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

items.content:
Day 9 — Maturity Levels: The Four Bands
 
Your score isn't a grade. It's a position on a map. Four bands, and the point of knowing yours is seeing what the next one looks like.
Reactive, 0 to 30%. Procurement is overhead. Decisions happen after something breaks. Single-source dependencies are a surprise, every quarter.
Functional, 31 to 60%. You have a defined role and basic KPIs, but procurement isn't part of strategy yet. Things work — until they don't.
Strategic, 61 to 85%. Procurement reports to a C-level. Goals tie to margin, growth, and working capital. Leadership consults you before the big moves. This is where most of my clients want to live.
Best-in-Class, 86 to 100%. Sourcing decisions shape pricing, product, and competitive position. Procurement is a profit center, not a cost center.
Most teams don't sit in one band. You might be Strategic in spend visibility and Reactive in risk. That spread is useful — it tells you exactly where to spend the next 90 days.
A good manufacturer can move two full bands in a single category in 90 days, mostly from agreeing on what good looked like and going after the gap.
Which band fits you today — and which one do you want to be in by year end?

Day 7 — Step 6: People & Capability

Every other category in this Health Check runs on this one. You can buy software and write policies. You cannot fake a team.
The honest question here is whether procurement is a career destination at your company or a firefighting station people flee. If your buyers spend more than 40% of their time expediting and putting out fires, you don't have a development problem. You have a retention bomb with a slow fuse. Good people don't leave for money as often as they leave because the work never stops feeling like an emergency.
The one that exposes everyone: if your best buyer left tomorrow, could the work continue? Or does half of what keeps the place running live in one person's head and inbox? Undocumented knowledge isn't job security for them. It's a single point of failure for you.
The Army taught me this before supply chain did. You build the bench before you need it, because the day you need it, it's too late to start.
If your strongest buyer gave notice this afternoon, how much would walk out the door with them?

items.content:
Step 3: Spend Visibility & Master Data
You can't negotiate what you can't see. And most mid-market manufacturers can't see their own spend without a two-day fire drill.
This category sounds like an IT problem. It isn't. It's a money problem wearing an IT costume. Dirty master data — duplicate suppliers, miscoded categories, three spellings of the same vendor — hides leverage. You think you have four suppliers in a category. You have one, billing you under four names, and you've been negotiating against yourself.
The test is simple. Can you pull a clean spend report by category, supplier, and buyer in under an hour? Not a clean-it-up-over-the-weekend report. An hour. If the answer is no, every sourcing decision you make is running on a guess.
The quiet killer here is tail spend — everything under $10K a transaction. It's usually a third of your supplier count and almost none of your attention. Ignored tail spend is where maverick buying lives.
Time yourself this week. Clean spend report, by category and supplier. How long did it actually take?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

Day 6 — Step 5: Risk & Resilience

There are two ways to find your single points of failure. On a spreadsheet, on a quiet Tuesday. Or on the floor, when the line stops and nobody can say why.
Resilience isn't a binder you write after an audit. It's whether you can name your top five supply chain risks right now, today, and point to a plan for each one. Most teams can name one — usually the one that already bit them.
The deeper miss is sub-tier visibility. You know your direct suppliers. Do you know who supplies them? The part shortage that stops your line often starts two tiers down, with a sub-supplier you've never heard of, in a country you didn't know you were exposed to.
I held 98.7% inventory availability through COVID while competitors went on allocation. That wasn't luck or a bigger checkbook. It was knowing where the single points of failure were before the world found out the hard way, and having moved on them first.
Tariffs are doing the same thing right now to companies that mapped exposure at the country level and stopped there.
Your top five risks. Can you name them without opening a file?

Most procurement self-assessments are built to make you feel good. This one isn't.
I kept walking into manufacturers — $50M to $500M, the companies I work with — and hearing the same line. “Our procurement is fine.” Then we'd pull the spend data. Tail spend nobody owned. Single-source dependencies nobody had mapped. A CEO who couldn't name one procurement KPI.
Fine is a feeling. I wanted a number.
So I built one. Thirty questions. Eight minutes. It's anchored in the two frameworks the Fortune 500 companies actually uses to score themselves — the ASCM SCOR Digital Standard and the ISM Capability Model — adapted down for what a mid-market manufacturer actually deals with. The questions are behavioral, not aspirational. Not “do you value supplier relationships.” Do you share a scorecard with your top suppliers every quarter. Yes or no.
That's the part that matters. Sandbag the score to feel better and you've thrown away the one thing the tool was going to give you — the gaps.
It scores six categories. Strategic Alignment. Sourcing & Supplier Management. Spend Visibility & Master Data. Process Discipline. Risk & Resilience. People & Capability.
Each one gets a subtotal. Add them up and you land in one of four maturity bands — Reactive, Functional, Strategic, Best-in-Class. Then the tool flags your three lowest categories. That's not a list of what you're bad at. That's where the money is. Most teams I work with are stronger than they think in one or two areas and quietly bleeding in another they've never measured.
A 60% in Risk & Resilience isn't a verdict on your team. It's a starting line. Manufacturers can move two full maturity bands in a category inside 90 days — mostly from finally agreeing on what “good” looked like and going after the gap.
Over the next nine posts I'm breaking the whole thing down. One category a day. The actual questions, and the trap each one is built to catch. Then the scoring, the bands, and where to start.
If you run procurement — or you're the CEO who signs off on it — follow along. By the end you'll score your own function without me in the room.

items.content:
Step 4: Process Discipline

Process discipline is invisible when things are calm. Then a line goes down at 4 p.m. on a Friday and you find out exactly how much of it you have.
The tell in this category is expedites. In a disciplined shop, an expedite gets approved before the supplier is authorized to ship. In an undisciplined one, the buyer makes the call under pressure, the freight bill shows up later, and finance asks who signed off. Nobody did. That's not a decision. It's an invoice you already owed.
Same story with contracts. If you've ever been surprised by an auto-renewal, you don't have a contract process — you have a drawer. Central tracking with renewal alerts costs almost nothing and saves you from negotiating with a gun to your head 30 days out.
Discipline isn't bureaucracy. It's what lets you move fast without breaking things, because everyone already knows the approval thresholds and the escalation path before the pressure hits.
When a supplier issue can't be solved at the buyer level, does everyone know exactly who it goes to next?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

items.content:
I was part of the first team at Finish Thompson to source directly from India. Here's what I wish I'd known before we started.
We qualified two Indian suppliers. First direct India sourcing the company had ever done. A lot went right. A few things were harder than expected. Here's the honest version:
What went well: The quality, once the suppliers understood our standards, was excellent. The suppliers we worked with were technically sophisticated, responsive, and genuinely interested in building a long-term relationship. India's manufacturing capability is often underestimated by companies that haven't been there. The pricing was competitive — not always dramatically lower than other Asian sources when you include freight and lead time, but competitive with the quality level we needed.
What was harder than I expected: Lead times are longer than China. Not dealbreaker-longer, but plan for it. Buffer inventory matters more here. Communication rhythm took adjustment. Not a capability issue — a time zone and process issue that smoothed out after the first few months once we'd established a regular cadence. First article qualification took longer than comparable processes with more experienced export suppliers. Build the extra time into your project plan and don't treat it as a problem — it's just the front-loaded investment in a relationship that pays off later.
The bottom line: India sourcing is real and it works. It's not a magic solution to tariff pressure, and it's not a backup you can stand up in 90 days. But as part of a diversified global supply strategy, done properly, it delivers. If you're looking at India as part of a China diversification strategy — I'm happy to share more about what the qualification process looked like. It's more accessible than most companies think.
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

items.content:
Step 2: Sourcing & Supplier Management
Most companies think they manage suppliers. What they actually do is place orders and hope.
Real supplier management means a scorecard. A real one, shared with your top suppliers every quarter, with on-time delivery, quality in PPM, and responsiveness on it. If your supplier has never seen the numbers you keep on them, you're not managing the relationship. You're just buying from it.
The trap in this category is the top-20 list. Most teams have one — by spend. Almost nobody has the second list, by criticality. Those are different suppliers. Your biggest invoice and your biggest risk rarely share a name. The $40K-a-year machine shop that makes the one part nobody else can make will hurt you worse than the million-dollar vendor with three backups.
When I ran a $63M book across 43 suppliers at GE Transportation, the ones that kept me up at night weren't the largest. They were the single-source specialists buried in the middle of the spend.
Pull your top 20 by spend. Now pull them by criticality. How much overlap did you actually get?

items.content:
The 4 Answers That Win Crisis Credibility

At GE, everyone had their number. One metric that determined whether you'd make your goals. For sourcing, it was cost savings — deflation. You'd plan a target and build the roadmap to get there. Then something would derail the plan.
You needed to recover. But you also needed to tell management in a way that inspired confidence instead of panic. Every plan hits roadblocks. The question is whether you can present that roadblock and your response clearly enough to drive action and keep leadership aligned.
I found that having these four answers, delivered crisply in two minutes, was highly effective:
What's the root cause? Tell management why you're in this situation. Did the supplier short ship? Are they demanding a price increase? Did engineering change a design? You don't need to go down to the smallest detail, but you need to put the problem in context. Someone else may have seen this before. If you can't define the issue clearly, management can't trust you to solve it.
When will we feel it? Everyone needs to understand the timeline. Will this hit the production line tomorrow at start-up, or is it a problem for next quarter? How much runway do you have to fix it? This drives resource allocation and gives everyone a deadline.
How much will it impact? Will the line shut down or will it be a hiccup? Will you miss your number by $5k or $500k? Let management know what they can expect if nothing gets fixed. Make sure they understand this is worst-case — you're already working on mitigation.
What's the plan? Your recovery doesn't need to be super-detailed, but you need to clearly spell out what you're doing. Is there another source? Are you escalating to their CEO? Who else is engaged? Without a recovery plan, you're just dropping a hot potato on someone else's lap.
When you can deliver these four data points clearly, you're well on your way to solving the problem. The tone matters as much as the content. Practice saying these cleanly so you sound strong in what you're saying. The more "ums" and "ahs," the less confident management feels in your ability to handle it.
Senior leaders have told me that once these four things are answered, they can't ask too many more questions. They're paying you to lead these issues. When you state your issues, the impact, your recovery plan in a firm, clear voice — you're assuring them their trust is well founded.
#SupplyChain #Leadership #Procurement

items.content:
How To Build Stakeholder Alignment Before You Decide

We had an incumbent vendor. Bad pricing, poor design, late delivery. The list was endless.
As the procurement leader, I knew I needed better options. But I didn't make that decision alone. I got the stakeholders in a room: Engineering, Manufacturing, Sales, Finance.
We built a scorecard together. Critical dimensions of what a perfect supplier would deliver. Weights for each dimension. Thresholds for selection. Most importantly — we agreed on what success would look like before we ever bid the market.
Then we went out, bid the commodity, and found something interesting: the incumbent was still the best fit.
But we had data for where they were falling short. We knew exactly what their competitors offered that they didn't.
This led to a frank conversation with the incumbent. "Here's where you're not meeting the market. Here's what we need from you." They came back with a price reduction, dedicated engineering resources on site, and a redesigned delivery system.
We got a better supplier and a better deal without switching vendors or spending six months on a transition.
Here's why this matters: when everyone in that room helped build the scorecard, they all had skin in the game. When the incumbent improved, they all saw it as a win. There was no second-guessing in the hallways.
Stakeholder alignment before the decision is harder than making it alone. It takes longer. It requires uncomfortable conversations with people who see the world differently. But it's the difference between a procurement decision and a company decision.
How have you met with your team to build better buying criteria?
#Procurement #Negotiation #SupplyChain #Manufacturing

items.content:
We reshored 121 SKUs from China. Zero production stoppages. 12% net cost reduction. Here's what actually worked.
I see a lot of LinkedIn posts that make reshoring sound impossible or trivial. It's neither. It's a methodical slog that rewards patience over heroics.
First: Rank the SKUs by difficulty and risk. How specialized is the tooling? How often do you actually run out of stock? What kills your operation if you run dry during transition? That ranked list becomes your project plan. Start with the easy wins. Don't start with the hardest ones just because they scare you.
Second: Build inventory before you move anything. We built 18 months of safety stock before we transferred a single mold. Expensive? Yeah. But it's the one decision that lets you move at the right pace instead of a panic pace. Most reshoring projects fail because someone's breathing down your neck.
Third: Move the knowledge, not just the contract. Molds, setup notes, first article inspection history — all of it. Most companies I've seen switch suppliers and leave all that institutional knowledge sitting with the old vendor. You've just traded one crisis for another.
Fourth: Don't qualify under pressure. We never qualified a mold with a hard production deadline attached to it. If the first article inspection found something, we had weeks to fix it. That breathing room is what kept us from shutting down the line.
Fifth: Do the full cost math. Material cost is higher domestically. But tariffs, freight, lead time, quality escapes, problem resolution — when you add it all up, ours came out 12% cheaper. The unit cost lied.
Every manufacturer is running this number right now. If you're figuring out where to start, I'm easy to find.
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

Step 1: Strategic Alignment
Ask a CEO if procurement matters and you'll get a “yes” every time. Ask the same CEO to name two or three procurement KPIs from memory, and the room goes quiet.
That gap is the whole category.
Strategic Alignment is the first step in the Health Check, and it's the one most teams overrate. It's not about whether leadership likes you. It's about whether procurement is in the room before the big calls get made — the new product line, the plant expansion, the customer you're about to commit capacity to. If you find out after, you're not aligned. You're cleaning up.
Four questions in this category. The one that catches people: are your savings targets tied to margin, working capital, or growth — or are you just chasing a savings number because someone set one? Savings for its own sake is how you end up cutting a supplier that was holding your best customer together.
At GE Transportation, I sat in on the decisions before they were final. That's why a $50M six-year motor contract got structured the way it did, instead of getting handed to procurement to go execute after the terms were locked.
Where does procurement sit at your company — in the room, or down the hall?

items.content:
The Army calls it a Hot Wash. Most companies call it a post-mortem. The difference? The Army actually does it every single time.

When I was an Army officer, we ran an After Action Report after every mission. Not just the ones that went wrong. Every. Single. One.

The format was simple: What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a gap? What do we do differently next time? Sometimes it was a brief as 3 ups, 3 downs.

No rank in the room during the debrief. The newest private could tell the commander what went wrong. That was the rule. Because the alternative — people staying quiet to protect egos — gets someone hurt next time.

I try to drive that same discipline into every supply chain role I’ve had since.

At one company, we had a supplier quality escape that shut down a production line for two days. Expensive. Embarrassing. The instinct was to fix it, move on, and pretend it didn’t happen.

Instead, we ran a Hot Wash. Got the procurement team, the quality team, and the production leads in one room. Walked through the timeline hour by hour.

What we found wasn’t a supplier problem. It was a receiving inspection gap — we’d changed the spec six months earlier and never updated the incoming inspection criteria. The supplier was building to the new spec. We were inspecting to the old one. The parts sat in quarantine for three weeks before anyone escalated.

That one Hot Wash led to a process change that prevented the same failure mode across every supplier in the network. Thirty minutes of uncomfortable conversation saved months of future downtime.

Here’s what I see at most companies: the crisis happens, everybody hustles to fix it, and then they wipe the sweat from their brow, congratulate each other, and move on to the next fire.

Nobody sits down and asks what actually broke. Or worse — they do sit down, but the meeting turns into a blamestorming session instead of a learning exercise.

The best procurement teams I’ve worked with have a system for this. Not a suggestion. A system. Every significant supplier issue gets a structured review within two weeks. Findings get documented. Changes get implemented. And the same mistake doesn’t happen twice.

Anyone can recover from a failure. What separates good companies from great ones is what happens in the 48 hours after.

When was the last time your team ran a real Hot Wash — not a blame session, but an honest debrief that actually changed how you operate?
#SupplyChain #Leadership #Procurement #StrategicSourcing

items.content:
Sometimes it's hard to know what your boss expects. That's why I created a user manual for my team.
Your annual goals and company objectives should be crystal clear. You should be discussing them weekly in your one-on-ones with your boss, and they should be driving your day-to-day work.
But the real question is never about the big goals.
It's about the small decisions. The unplanned fire you need to put out. The gray area where you have to act but you can't check in on everything. What's your frame of reference?
I had a leader who asked their management team to create a few bullet points describing what they actually care about — not the HR version, but the real version. What would the team do if they had to make a decision with zero guidance? I've come to call it my "user manual."
These are the five critical behaviors I expect from my team:
·       Open, clear communication
·       Momentum Driven
·       Check your ego
·       You own your deck
·       Prioritize & Execute
We go through these in the first week. I reference them all year in feedback conversations. It's not a one-time thing — we talk about it constantly.
Here's the thing: it cuts both ways.
I tell my team this is what to expect from me. And I make it clear that they have an obligation to call me out when I'm not living up to these values. I can't hold them accountable to standards I'm not performing to. We hold each other to these things.
That's the difference between a list on a page and something that actually shapes how a team works.
Does your team know what's in your user manual?
#Leadership #FractionalCPO #Procurement

items.content:
A supplier walked into our negotiation asking for a price increase. We pulled up their own website. It was bragging about record profits. You could see the color drain from their faces.

Here’s the full story:

When I was at GE, we negotiated electronic component pricing as an enterprise — consolidating volume across divisions to get the best deals. We’d meet with major manufacturers twice a year to set pricing for the next six months. Millions of dollars on the table every session.

One manufacturer came in asking for price increases across the board. Not a small ask — this would have cost us millions.

Their pitch was polished. Costs were up. Raw materials were squeezing margins. They needed capital investment to keep pace with production. The whole story sounded reasonable.

Then the lead negotiator on our side opened a laptop and pulled up the manufacturer’s own website.

Their investor page was celebrating record profits. Their press releases touted cost-cutting measures that had driven margins to all-time highs. They had glossy photos of the brand-new high-speed machines that had reduced their labor costs.

We asked them to square what was on the screen with what they had just told us.

There was nothing they could say.

The supplier agreed to a price reduction. Their own words had made the case for us.

The lesson: The best leverage in a negotiation isn’t volume or threats. It’s preparation. When you walk in with data — benchmarks, public filings, their own press releases — the conversation changes completely. You’re not arguing opinion against opinion. You’re presenting facts.

The negotiator who’s done the homework rarely has to raise their voice.

When has doing your homework given you an unexpected edge in a negotiation?

We needed 3 lbs of powder coating material. Nobody on the continent had it. I found it in a lab in Germany.
My first battalion commander as a young Army officer had a rule for all leaders: "Ignore the first 5 'No's' when it comes to soldier welfare."
He expected us to leave no stone unturned when it came to taking care of the troops. That lesson stuck. I've carried it into every supply chain role since — for my team and for the customer. It's been behind a few miracles over 25 years.
Here's one of them:
We had an emergency takeover for a customer that was going to be held up by one part. A collar needed powder coating in a very specific color and grade. We needed 3 lbs to complete the run.
The powder coater didn't have it. Wasn't sure when he'd get it.
That's No #1. Most people stop here.
I got the powder coat sales company's contact info and called them. They were waiting on an update from their distributor. I got the distributor's number and called them directly.
No #2.
Distribution was waiting for a shipment from Germany. Best guess: 3-4 weeks. Nothing else in the pipeline at other coaters.
No #3.
I asked for the manufacturer's name, tracked down their headquarters in Germany, and made an early morning call across the Atlantic.
Everything was in transit. The coating wasn't scheduled to run for another 4 months.
No #4.
I asked about lab samples — we only needed a small amount. The contact said he'd check.
40 very tense minutes later, Germany called back. They had a 3 lb sample they could drop ship to the coater in 2 days. I gave them our small pack account, called the coater, called the customer, and the run stayed on schedule.
Everyone thought I was a miracle worker.
I thought it was just another day of ignoring the first 5 No's.
Here's the thing most procurement teams get wrong: they treat the first "no" like a wall. It's not a wall. It's a door to someone who might know the answer. And behind that door is another door. The people who solve the impossible problems are the ones willing to keep knocking.
Does your procurement team stop at the first No — or do they ignore the first five?

The most powerful thing you can do in a supplier negotiation is stop talking.
I mean it. After 25 years and over $150 million in contracts, this is the one tactic that has never once failed me.
Here's how it works:
You present your position. Your data. Your benchmark. Your ask.
And then you stop.
The silence feels unbearable. Every instinct tells you to fill it. To soften the ask. To explain yourself further. To offer a concession they haven't even asked for yet.
Don't.
The first person who speaks after a proposal has been made is the person who concedes ground. Almost every time.
I've watched experienced procurement professionals negotiate beautifully for 45 minutes — build the case, present the data, make a strong ask — and then give away 2% in the final ten seconds because the silence made them uncomfortable.
Two percent on a $10M spend is $200,000. That's the cost of not being able to sit quietly for 30 seconds.
Here's why it works: silence puts the pressure on the other party to respond to your position. The moment you keep talking, you're responding to your own position — and usually making it weaker.
The supplier is thinking. Let them think. That's the whole point.
I tell my team: after you make the ask, put your pen down. Take a sip of water. Look at your notes. Do whatever you need to do — just don't talk.
The answer will come. And it will almost always be better than whatever you were about to say to fill the gap.
What's the hardest part of negotiation for you — the preparation, the conversation, or the silence?

Think back to the last time you had to take charge of a floundering effort. Something important was falling apart. Nobody was going to fix it except you.
Was it because you were the only one with the horsepower? Did someone misunderstand your intent and go sideways? Was the team not ready for the responsibility?
Here's the hard part: as leaders, we need to be able to delegate. If we can't trust our team with critical work, we're burning ourselves out.
But when you do step in — and sometimes you will — the question isn't just "how do I fix this." It's "what went wrong that forced me to step in."
Did the team identify the root cause of the failure? Or did everyone just rush to fix the symptom and move on?
Did you take time to put systems in place to ensure you could hand it off next time and know it would work? Or are you setting up the same failure to happen again?
Here's what I've learned: taking time to ensure everyone has the knowledge, authority, and clarity for the tasks they're responsible for is a force multiplier. It keeps you from having to jump in. And when you do jump in, it gives you a clear picture of what actually broke.
The best leaders I've worked with don't minimize the number of times they have to take over a project. They minimize the second time the same thing happens.
When was the last time you had to step in — and what did you learn about your team from that moment?
